610.title: Upasiva's question
610.hook: one of the sixteen asks what to rely on to cross; the Buddha answers, nothingness, mindfully
610.howItsDone: Teachers often cite Upasiva's question when explaining nibbana as the flame gone out, and the image of the flame that can no longer be reckoned is common in Theravada teaching on what can and cannot be said of the awakened.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an old teacher's sixteen students on the road north, and your line, crossing the flood. Did you carry your question around with you? Today, one of the sixteen asks his. Day six hundred ten.

Upasiva is the sixth of the sixteen to speak. His question is short, and it's the most honest thing anyone says in the whole chapter. Alone, he says, with nothing to hold on to, I can't cross the great flood. Tell me something to lean on. Anyone who has stood at the edge of something too big, a diagnosis, a debt, a loss, knows that sentence. Not what is the meaning of life. Just: what do I hold? Today: Upasiva's question.
screen: `THE SIXTH OF THE SIXTEEN.` → `ALONE, I CAN'T CROSS.` → `TELL ME SOMETHING TO LEAN ON.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's answer is surprising. Mindful, he says, looking to nothingness, leaning on the thought there is nothing, cross the flood. Let go of sense-desires, step back from talk, and watch, day and night, for the end of craving. Upasiva had meditated deeply; the commentary says he already knew the meditation called the base of nothingness. So the Buddha meets him there, in the place he already knows, and adds the one thing that turns it from a resting place into a crossing: mindfulness. Upasiva asks more. If someone stays there, does he go cold, or is he freed? The Buddha gives an image. As a flame blown out by the wind goes to rest and can't be counted any more, so the sage, freed, goes to rest and can't be counted. Does he not exist then, Upasiva asks, or is he forever well? There's no measuring the one who has gone to rest, the Buddha says. When everything is uprooted, every way of speaking about him is uprooted too. That last answer is famous because it refuses both easy options. And with it, we close the Sutta Nipata: from the snake shedding its skin, through the herdsman in the rain, the rhinoceros, the jewel, the blessings, the poet, the dart, the eights, all the way to this crossing. Tomorrow, a new book, of joy.
screen: `MINDFUL, LOOKING TO NOTHINGNESS.` · `MEETING HIM WHERE HE IS.` · `A FLAME BLOWN OUT BY THE WIND.` · `NO MEASURING THE ONE AT REST.` · then, large: `MINDFUL, CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rely on mindfulness today. Sit and settle. Notice what you usually lean on when things get hard: your phone, a plan, someone's reassurance. You don't have to give any of them up. Just, for these two minutes, lean on nothing but knowing what's happening. Breath in, known. Breath out, known. A sound, known. When the mind reaches for a handhold, notice the reaching, and come back. The bell holds the time.
Upasiva's question. One of the sixteen asks what to lean on to cross the flood, and is told: mindful, looking to nothingness, cross. Today's word.
Your line: mindful, cross. Today, when something feels too big, take one step with full attention, and let that step be enough. Day six hundred ten.

611.title: Inspired sayings
611.hook: short verses the Buddha spoke from joy, each with its story
611.howItsDone: The Udana is read and taught in Theravada communities, and its verses are sometimes chanted; Sanskrit-language schools kept a related collection called the Udanavarga, which is close to the Dhammapada.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upasiva's question, the flame gone out, and your line, mindful, cross. Did one step with full attention feel like enough? The Sutta Nipata is behind us. Today a new book opens. Day six hundred eleven.

Some things you say on purpose. Others just come out. You round a bend on a hike and the whole valley opens, and before you've decided anything you've said, oh. A friend tells you good news and you laugh out loud. Those words aren't planned. They're breathed out. The early Buddhist canon has a whole book built from moments like that: times when something happened, the Buddha saw what it meant, and a few lines of verse came out of him. The book takes its name from that breathing out. Today: the Udana, inspired sayings.
screen: `SOME WORDS JUST COME OUT.` → `THE VALLEY OPENS: OH.` → `A BOOK OF THOSE MOMENTS.`

segments.voice: Udana comes from a root that has to do with breathing out, and it came to mean a heartfelt utterance, words spoken from a full heart, often from joy. The book is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of short books, alongside the Dhammapada and the Sutta Nipata you've just finished. It has eighty discourses, arranged in eight chapters of ten. And every one follows the same shape, which makes it easy to read. First, a short story in prose: where the Buddha was, who came, what happened. Then a formula, repeated eighty times: knowing the meaning of this, the Buddha, on that occasion, spoke this inspired saying. Then the verse. So the story is the soil and the verse is what grows from it. The stories are often small and human: a woman in a long, hard labor; a monk homesick for his bride; boys at a pond; moths at a lamp. A few are among the deepest passages in the canon, and you'll meet them in the coming days. One more thing. Not every udana is joyful in the way we mean it. Some come from sorrow, some from seeing something hard. But all of them come from seeing clearly, and in the text that clear seeing is itself a kind of gladness.
screen: `UDANA: A BREATHING OUT.` · `EIGHTY DISCOURSES, EIGHT CHAPTERS.` · `FIRST THE STORY, THEN THE VERSE.` · `SMALL STORIES, DEEP VERSES.` · then, large: `SPOKEN FROM JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one udana, and before that, sit with one. Settle. Think back over the past week for a moment when something made you breathe out: a sky, a kindness, a child saying something unexpected. Let the scene come back, the place, the light. Notice what it meant to you. You don't need words for it. Just let the breath go out slowly, the way it did then. After the bell, if you like, find one udana and read it. The bell holds the time.
Udana. An inspired saying, words breathed out from a full heart; and the name of a book of eighty short stories, each ending in a verse. Today's word.
Your line: spoken from joy. Today, when something makes you breathe out, notice it, and let yourself say it, even if it's only to yourself. Day six hundred eleven.

612.title: Doubts vanish
612.hook: after awakening he reviews dependent origination, and doubts vanish like mist
612.tomorrow: In the seen, only the seen
612.howItsDone: Dependent origination is studied in every Buddhist tradition, and in many Theravada monasteries its links are chanted in forward and reverse order, as in the opening of the Udana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Udana, a book of words breathed out, and your line, spoken from joy. Did something make you breathe out? Today, the very first udana, from the first week after the awakening. Day six hundred twelve.

The book doesn't start with a crowd or a sermon. It starts under a tree. The Buddha has just awakened, at Uruvela, on the bank of the Neranjara river, at the foot of the tree we now call the bodhi tree. And for seven days, the text says, he sits there in one cross-legged posture, feeling the happiness of release. No teaching yet. No students. Just a man sitting by a river for a week. At the end of those seven days, he does something very specific with his mind, through the watches of the night. Today: doubts vanish.
screen: `UNDER THE TREE, BY THE RIVER.` → `SEVEN DAYS IN ONE POSTURE.` → `THEN, THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In the first watch of the night, he attends to dependent origination in forward order: when this is, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. Ignorance gives rise to formations, formations to consciousness, and so on, link by link, to the whole mass of suffering. And the verse comes: when things become clear to the one who meditates with ardor, his doubts all vanish, because he understands a thing together with its cause. The next udana: the same, in reverse. When this is not, that does not come to be; with the ending of this, that ends. Doubts vanish, because he understands the ending of causes. The third: both directions together. And this time the verse adds an image: he stands, scattering Mara's army, like the sun lighting up the sky. Notice how doubt goes in this story. Not by being argued with. Not by being pushed down. It goes because something is seen: this comes from that. Doubt in the early texts is one of the five hindrances, the wobbling that can't decide. What ends it isn't certainty about everything. It's seeing one cause clearly. Mist doesn't need to be fought. The sun comes up, and it's gone.
screen: `FORWARD: THIS ARISES FROM THAT.` · `BACKWARD: THIS ENDS WITH THAT.` · `BOTH, AND MARA'S ARMY SCATTERS.` · `SEEING A CAUSE ENDS DOUBT.` · then, large: `DOUBTS VANISH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace one cause. Sit and settle. Pick one feeling that's here right now: a bit of tiredness, worry, a flicker of irritation. Ask, gently, where did this come from? Maybe a short night. Maybe a message you read. Follow it one link back, then one more if it's there. Don't analyze too hard. Just see: this came from that. Notice whether the feeling changes when its cause is seen. The bell holds the time.
Doubts vanish. The first three udanas: when the Buddha sees how each thing arises from its cause, his doubts vanish, and in the third verse he shines like the sun lighting up the sky. Today's word.
Your line: doubts vanish. Today, when you can't decide something, look for one cause underneath it, and see if the fog thins. Day six hundred twelve.

attend to how each thing arises from its cause, through the night.

what a scholar hears: Udana 1.1–1.3 review paticcasamuppada forward (anuloma), reverse (patiloma) and both, a sequence also found at the opening of the Vinaya's Mahavagga.

613.title: In the seen, only the seen
613.hook: to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard
613.carry: in the seen, only the seen
613.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in Theravada and other traditions often give the Bahiya instruction as a practice of bare attention: noting what is seen, heard, sensed and known, without adding to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three watches of the night under the tree, and your line, doubts vanish. Did seeing one cause thin the fog? Today, a teaching only a few lines long, given on a city street. Day six hundred thirteen.

On the coast at Supparaka lives a man called Bahiya of the bark cloth, because he dresses in strips of bark. People honor him; they bring him food and robes; many think he's fully awakened. One day he wonders it himself. And a deity who wishes him well, the text says, tells him plainly: you're not, and you're not even on the way. But in Savatthi, far to the north, there's someone who is. Bahiya sets out at once. The text says he never stayed more than one night anywhere on the way. He arrives at the monastery and is told: the Teacher has gone into town for alms. So he follows him into the street. Today: in the seen, only the seen.
screen: `BAHIYA OF THE BARK CLOTH.` → `YOU'RE NOT EVEN ON THE WAY.` → `HE FOLLOWS HIM INTO THE STREET.`

segments.voice: Bahiya finds the Buddha walking for alms, falls at his feet, and asks: teach me. The Buddha says, it's not the time; we've come into town for alms. Bahiya asks again, and gives his reason: life is uncertain, yours and mine. Not the time, the Buddha says again. A third time Bahiya asks. And there, in the street, with the alms bowl in his hand, the Buddha gives him a teaching only a few lines long. Train yourself like this, Bahiya. In the seen, there will be only the seen. In the heard, only the heard. In the sensed, only the sensed. In the known, only the known. When that's so, you won't be with it. When you're not with it, you won't be in it. Then you'll be neither here nor beyond nor in between. That is the end of suffering. What does it mean? Look at the first line. You see a face in a crowd. And instantly the mind adds: she's frowning at me, I must have done something, I always do this. The seen was a face. Everything else was added. The teaching asks Bahiya to stop at the face. Not to stop seeing, but to stop building on top of it. When nothing is added, there's no I standing in the middle of it all, taking it personally. Then the Buddha walks on with his bowl. What happens to Bahiya next is tomorrow's story.
screen: `THREE TIMES HE ASKS.` · `IN THE STREET, WITH THE BOWL.` · `SEEN, HEARD, SENSED, KNOWN.` · `NOTHING ADDED, NO ONE IN THE MIDDLE.` · then, large: `IN THE SEEN, ONLY THE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see without adding. Sit with your eyes open, resting on something near you: a cup, a patch of wall. Let it be only what's seen: color, shape, light. When the mind adds a name, a story, an opinion, just notice: that's added. Come back to color and shape. Then close your eyes and do the same with sound: only the heard. A car is just a rising and falling sound. The bell holds the time.
In the seen. The Buddha's teaching to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; nothing added, and no one in the middle. Today's word.
Your line: in the seen, only the seen. Today, when someone's face or tone starts a story in you, stop at the face, and let the story wait. Day six hundred thirteen.

what it means: stop at what the senses give; when nothing is added, there's no self standing in the middle to take it personally.
what a scholar hears: the four (dittha, suta, muta, vinnata: seen, heard, sensed, known) recur in the canon; the same instruction is given to Malunkyaputta in SN 35.95.

614.title: No time to lose
614.hook: Bahiya awakens on the spot, and dies soon after, gored by a cow
614.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell Bahiya's story to illustrate appamada, heedfulness, and in many Theravada communities he is remembered as the disciple foremost in quick understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bahiya in the street, and your line, in the seen, only the seen. Did you stop at a face and let the story wait? Today, what happened to Bahiya next. Day six hundred fourteen.

Most of us have a someday list. Someday I'll call my aunt. Someday I'll start sitting every morning. Someday I'll say sorry for that thing in college. The list feels safe because it assumes there's time. Bahiya didn't assume it. When the Buddha told him twice that it wasn't the time, Bahiya's answer was blunt: life is uncertain, yours and mine. He'd crossed a whole country to hear the teaching, and he wasn't willing to wait until after lunch. Yesterday you heard what he was told. Today, how the story ends, and why it ends so fast. Today: no time to lose.
screen: `THE SOMEDAY LIST.` → `LIFE IS UNCERTAIN, YOURS AND MINE.` → `NOT AFTER LUNCH.`

segments.voice: The text says that as he heard those few lines, in the seen only the seen, Bahiya's mind was freed, right there in the street. Then the Buddha went on with his alms round. And not long after, a cow with a young calf attacked Bahiya and killed him. That's the whole of it, in one sentence. On his way back, the Buddha saw the body. He asked the monks to carry it on a litter, to cremate it, and to build a memorial mound for him. When the monks asked what had become of Bahiya, the Buddha said: he was wise; he practiced in line with the teaching; he didn't trouble me with questions about it. He has reached final release. Elsewhere in the canon, in a list of outstanding disciples, Bahiya is named foremost among those who understood quickly. Sit with the shape of the story for a moment. A man traveled far, asked three times, heard a few lines, understood them, and died the same morning. If he had waited for the right time, there would have been no time. The early texts have a word for this kind of alertness: appamada, heedfulness, not letting things slide. It doesn't mean panic. Bahiya wasn't frantic; he was clear. It means the good thing you can do today is today's.
screen: `FREED, RIGHT THERE IN THE STREET.` · `A COW WITH A YOUNG CALF.` · `FOREMOST IN QUICK UNDERSTANDING.` · `IF HE HAD WAITED.` · then, large: `NO TIME TO LOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't delay the good. Sit and settle. Let your someday list come to mind, and look for one item on it that's small: a message, a thank you, an apology, a few minutes of sitting. Pick that one. Picture yourself doing it today, where and when. Then let it go and rest with the breath, knowing it's waiting for you. Calm, not hurried. The bell holds the time.
No time to lose. Bahiya asked to be taught at once, because life is uncertain; he understood that morning and died the same day. Today's word.
Your line: no time to lose. Today, take the one small good thing off your someday list and do it before the evening. Day six hundred fourteen.

615.title: The boys and the fish
615.hook: boys tormenting fish; would you want pain?
615.howItsDone: The first of the five precepts many Buddhists keep is to refrain from killing or harming living beings, and teachers often explain it, as here, by putting oneself in the other's place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of Bahiya's story, and your line, no time to lose. Did one thing come off the someday list? Today, a scene by the road, and one question. Day six hundred fifteen.

Anyone who has watched kids at the edge of a pond knows how it can go. A stick, a jar, a dare. Somebody pokes at a frog to see it jump. Nobody's being evil; they're curious, and bored, and in a group. The Udana has a scene like that. The Buddha is walking between the city of Savatthi and the monastery at Jeta's Grove, and on the way he sees a crowd of boys tormenting fish. He could walk past. He could scold. He does neither. He stops, and asks them a question. Today: the boys and the fish.
screen: `A STICK, A JAR, A DARE.` → `ON THE ROAD TO JETA'S GROVE.` → `HE STOPS AND ASKS.`

segments.voice: Boys, he says, are you afraid of pain? Do you dislike pain? Yes, sir, they say. We're afraid of pain. We don't like it. That's all. Two questions, two honest answers. And then, knowing the meaning of it, he speaks the verse. If you fear pain, if you dislike pain, don't do a bad deed, openly or in secret. If you do, or are doing one, you won't be free of pain, even if you run and fly away. Notice the teaching method. He doesn't begin with the fish. He begins with the boys. He doesn't tell them what fish feel; he asks what they feel. And once they've said it out loud, the rest follows on its own: if you don't like pain, you already know something about everyone who can feel it. The Dhammapada has the same insight in its chapter on punishment: everyone trembles at the rod; putting yourself in their place, don't strike or cause to strike. The Udana gives it a scene and a pond. Notice, too, that the verse doesn't threaten the boys with a stranger's punishment. It points at the plain logic of cause and result: what you do follows you, even if you run. That's the same thread that's run through these weeks: by deeds, the rod and fear, and now this.
screen: `ARE YOU AFRAID OF PAIN?` · `START WITH THE BOYS, NOT THE FISH.` · `OPENLY OR IN SECRET.` · `EVEN IF YOU RUN.` · then, large: `ALL DISLIKE PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop one small cruelty. Sit and settle. Ask yourself the Buddha's question, honestly: do I dislike pain? Feel the answer in the body. Then let your mind go outward: a coworker, a stranger on the bus, a dog in the street, a fish in a pond. Each of them would answer the same. Now look for one small cruelty in your own day, a cutting joke, an impatient shove, a creature swatted without thinking. Just see it. Today, you can leave it undone. The bell holds the time.
The boys and the fish. In the Udana, the Buddha asks boys tormenting fish whether they dislike pain, and lets their answer teach them. Today's word.
screen: `THE BOYS AND THE FISH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: all dislike pain. Today, before one sharp act or word, ask yourself his question first: would I want this? Day six hundred fifteen.

616.title: Dearer than oneself
616.hook: King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika agree no one is dearer than oneself; so harm no other
616.howItsDone: Teachers of metta, loving-kindness, often begin with goodwill toward oneself and then extend the same wish to others, and many cite the verse to Pasenadi and Mallika as the reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boys by the pond, and your line, all dislike pain. Did you ask his question before one sharp act? Today closes a week, with a king and a queen on a palace roof. Day six hundred sixteen.

Picture a married couple on a rooftop terrace in the evening, the city spread out below. It's the kind of moment when one of them asks a question that's half tender and half a test. That's how this udana begins. King Pasenadi of Kosala, whom you've met kissing the Buddha's feet, is on the upper terrace of his palace with Queen Mallika. And he asks her: Mallika, is there anyone dearer to you than yourself? It's not hard to imagine what answer a husband might hope for. The text doesn't tell us what he hoped. It tells us what she said. Today: dearer than oneself.
screen: `A ROOFTOP AT EVENING.` → `A TENDER QUESTION, AND A TEST.` → `IS ANYONE DEARER THAN YOURSELF?`

segments.voice: No, your majesty, Mallika says. There is no one dearer to me than myself. And is there anyone dearer to you than yourself? The king thinks, and says: no, Mallika, for me too, there is no one dearer than myself. It's a startlingly honest exchange between two people who, by other accounts, loved each other. Pasenadi goes down from the palace and tells the Buddha. And the Buddha, knowing the meaning of this, speaks the verse. Searching all directions with the mind, one finds no one anywhere dearer than oneself. In the same way, each person holds themselves dear. So one who loves himself should not harm another. Look at what just happened. Something that sounds selfish, I love myself most, turns in two lines into the ground of kindness. The verse doesn't scold the king and queen for their honesty. It takes their honesty and turns it outward. If it's true for me, it's true for everyone. That's why the carry is everyone loves themselves. Look back at the week. Upasiva's crossing. The Udana opens. Doubts vanish under the tree. Bahiya in the street, and no time to lose. The boys at the pond. And now the palace roof.
